title: IMPORTANT
content: This manual is an educational reference. Local laws, state regulations, provincial regulations, national regulations, manufacturer instructions, permit conditions, and health department requirements always take priority over any recommendation in this book. When requirements conflict: Follow applicable law. Follow health department requirements. Follow equipment manufacturer instructions. Use this manual as supplemental guidance. The CDC Model Aquatic Health Code is intended as a science-based model that jurisdictions may adopt in whole, in part, or modify. It is not automatically law. (CDC)

title: 1.1 Purpose of This Manual
content: Welcome. This manual is designed to help commercial pool operators develop practical operating skills while also providing structured study support for operator training programs. It focuses on the daily responsibilities required to operate a commercial swimming pool safely, consistently, and professionally. The primary goals of this manual are to help you: Operate commercial aquatic facilities safely. Understand why operating procedures exist. Learn the basic science behind water treatment. Perform routine inspections with confidence. Respond appropriately to common operating problems. Develop the calculation skills needed for everyday operation. Build knowledge that supports professional certification preparation. This manual emphasizes operational competence rather than memorization. Every chapter is organized so that you can apply the information immediately during inspections, maintenance, and water testing. The recommendations throughout this book are based on publicly available guidance from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), particularly the Model Aquatic Health Code (MAHC), together with public educational information from CDC Healthy Swimming resources and publicly available descriptions of the Certified Pool Operator (CPO) program. The MAHC is guidance—not federal law—and becomes enforceable only if adopted by a local authority. Always follow the requirements that apply in your jurisdiction. (CDC)

content: Recreational pools are designed for general public use. They often serve the widest variety of bathers. Typical users include: Families Children Adults Senior citizens Operator focus: Water quality Patron supervision Deck safety Routine cleaning Bather hygiene education Typical risks: Crowding Contamination events Slip-and-fall injuries Horseplay

title: 5.6 Leisure Pools
content: Leisure pools emphasize recreation rather than lap swimming. Common features include: Beach entries Variable depths Waterfalls Play structures Spray effects Current channels These attractions often increase maintenance requirements. Operator focus: Inspect moving water features. Verify circulation in shallow areas. Remove debris frequently. Observe child activity.

title: 5.7 Activity Pools
content: Activity pools are designed for organized recreation. Examples include: Water volleyball Aquatic exercise Instructional programs Group activities Characteristics: Moderate depth Open floor area Frequent user interaction Operational considerations: Increased physical activity may increase contaminant loading. Equipment used during classes should be cleaned and stored properly. Schedule inspections between programs.

title: 5.8 Diving Pools
content: Diving pools support springboard or platform diving. Characteristics: Greater water depth Specialized diving equipment Lower swimmer density during individual dives Operator responsibilities: Do: Verify diving equipment condition. Inspect ladders and platforms. Maintain required clear water visibility. Prevent unauthorized diving. Typical risks: Head injuries Neck injuries Impact injuries Improper diving behavior

title: 5.9 Therapy Pools
content: Therapy pools support rehabilitation or therapeutic exercise. Typical users may include: Older adults Rehabilitation patients Individuals recovering from injury People with limited mobility Characteristics: Warmer water Lower-impact activities Specialized accessibility features Operator focus: Monitor temperature carefully. Maintain consistent water chemistry. Inspect accessibility equipment. Coordinate maintenance around therapy schedules.

title: 5.10 Spa Pools (Hot Tubs)
content: Spa pools operate differently from swimming pools. Characteristics include: Small water volume Elevated temperature Air injection Water jets High turbulence These conditions can increase disinfectant demand and require close operational attention. Operator focus: Monitor disinfectant frequently. Monitor pH regularly. Verify circulation. Inspect suction fittings. Check water level. Maintain filtration. Typical risks: Elevated microbial growth if disinfectant is inadequate. Chemical imbalance. Entrapment hazards. Overheating of bathers. Operators should encourage patrons to follow posted guidance regarding safe spa use.

title: 5.11 Interactive Water Play Venues
content: Interactive water play venues are commonly known as splash pads or spray parks. Unlike swimming pools, users generally do not immerse themselves in standing water. Common features include: Spray nozzles Ground jets Water cannons Interactive fountains Many systems recirculate treated water, while others may use continuously supplied potable water depending on local design and regulations. Operator focus: Verify spray operation. Maintain treatment systems. Inspect drain areas. Monitor water quality where water is recirculated. Clean spray surfaces. Typical risks: Surface contamination Biofilm development Slip hazards Inadequate disinfection where applicable

title: 5.12 Wading Pools
content: Wading pools are intended for young children. Characteristics: Very shallow water High caregiver presence Frequent contamination events Young children generally have increased accidental fecal release risk compared with older swimmers. Operator focus: Increase water testing frequency as needed. Encourage diaper-changing in designated areas. Clean surrounding surfaces frequently. Respond immediately to contamination incidents.

title: 5.13 Wave Pools
content: Wave pools generate artificial waves. Operational challenges include: Large water volume Complex circulation Mechanical wave equipment Variable bather movement Operator focus: Inspect wave-generation equipment. Monitor visibility. Observe crowd movement. Verify emergency stop systems. Coordinate with lifeguards. Typical risks: Collision injuries Fatigue Reduced visibility during heavy wave action

title: 5.14 Lazy Rivers
content: Lazy rivers move water continuously around a loop. Characteristics: Long hydraulic paths Continuous circulation Multiple entry points Floating devices Operator priorities: Monitor flow. Inspect pumps. Remove floating debris. Verify water circulation throughout the entire channel. Typical risks: Congestion Entrapment around inlets Slip hazards at entries and exits

title: 5.15 Water Slides
content: Water slides combine mechanical systems with aquatic landing areas. Components include: Launch platform Slide flume Water supply Landing pool or run-out channel Operator focus: Inspect slide surfaces. Verify water flow. Check dispatch procedures. Inspect barriers and stairs. Monitor rider spacing. Typical risks: Collision injuries Improper rider position Slip hazards Mechanical failures affecting water delivery

title: 5.16 Increased-Risk Aquatic Venues
content: The MAHC recognizes that certain aquatic venues or user populations may present increased public health concerns. Examples may include venues serving: Very young children Older adults Individuals requiring therapeutic services Users with increased susceptibility to illness These facilities may require enhanced operational attention because contamination events or disease transmission can have greater consequences. Operator focus: Maintain excellent water quality. Perform frequent monitoring. Follow contamination response procedures. Encourage healthy swimming practices. Maintain accurate operational records. Local regulations determine any additional requirements.

title: 5.17 Why Water Chemistry Changes Between Venue Types
content: Different venues consume disinfectant at different rates. Factors include: Water temperature Organic contamination Aeration Bather density Water agitation Exposure to sunlight Operating hours Examples: A spa with warm water and heavy use will typically consume disinfectant more rapidly than a cool lap pool with fewer users. A children's play venue may experience more frequent contamination events than an adult lap pool. These examples illustrate operational differences rather than fixed rules.

title: 5.18 Formula: Bather Density
content: Some facilities monitor how heavily a venue is being used. A simple educational calculation is: Bather Density = Number of Bathers / Water Surface Area Worked Example: Pool surface area = 4,000 square feet Current bathers = 80 Bather Density = 80 / 4,000 = 0.02 bathers per square foot This calculation is useful for internal operational awareness.

title: Chapter 6 — Units and Conversions
content: Chapter 6 — Units and Conversions

title: 6.0 Purpose and Scope
content: This chapter trains you to move correctly between the units you will encounter on a pool deck: gallons, liters, cubic feet, ppm/mg/L, and surface area. Every dosing calculation, water-balance adjustment, and volume estimate you perform later in this manual depends on getting this chapter right first. A unit error here does not stay small — it multiplies straight into a chemical dose or a turnover-rate calculation and can turn a correct formula into an unsafe one. Do treat this chapter as a skills chapter, not a reference chapter. Work every conversion by hand at least once before trusting a calculator or app to do it for you. You need to be able to catch a wrong answer, not just produce one.

title: 1 ppm = 1 mg/L
content: This works because "parts per million" is a mass-per-mass ratio, and one liter of water has a mass of approximately 1,000,000 mg (1 kg = 1,000 g = 1,000,000 mg) at everyday pool temperatures. A concentration expressed as milligrams of a substance dissolved in one liter of water is, by definition, one part in a million parts of water by mass. This equivalence is the standard convention used in water-treatment education and is why test kits and chemical labels use "ppm" and "mg/L" interchangeably for pool water.

hierarchy_path: Ch6/6.4.3 Worked Example — Total Mass of a Chemical in a Pool
title: 6.4.3 Worked Example — Total Mass of a Chemical in a Pool
content: A pool holds 20,000 gallons. You want to know the total mass of chlorine present at a reading of 3 ppm. Step 1 — Convert gallons to liters: 20,000 gal × 3.78541 = 75,708 L Step 2 — Apply the mg/L concentration: 75,708 L × 3 mg/L = 227,124 mg Step 3 — Convert to grams: 227,124 mg ÷ 1,000 = 227.1 g Step 4 — Convert to ounces if needed: 227.1 g × 0.035274 = 8.01 oz

title: Key Checks
content: [ ] All values in a single calculation are in the same unit system before any math is performed. [ ] Chemical label units (weight vs. volume, % strength) are matched to the formula being used. [ ] ppm/mg/L equivalence is applied only to dilute aqueous solutions. [ ] Surface area and volume are not substituted for one another. [ ] Freeform-area estimates are labeled as estimates, not used for code-driven decisions. [ ] Numeric targets are checked against local code and product label before use.

title: Common Mistakes
content: Multiplying a gallon figure by a metric conversion factor meant for cubic feet, or vice versa. Treating ppm and mg/L as different quantities that need converting into each other (they don't, for pool water). Using a diameter value where the formula calls for a radius (circular area errors). Confusing total surface area with total volume when sizing a cover or estimating bather load. Dropping the intermediate calculation step, making it impossible to audit an error later. Applying a percentage-strength conversion for a liquid chemical to a dry, granular product (or the reverse).

title: When to Call a Professional
content: When an irregular pool shape needs an area or volume figure for a code-required determination (permit, bather-load capacity, variance application) — request an as-built survey or licensed engineer's figure rather than a field estimate. When a chemical supplier's delivery documentation uses unit conventions you cannot reconcile with your facility's dosing records — contact the supplier or a certified water-treatment consultant before dosing. When metric and US customary equipment are mixed at a single site and staff report inconsistent readings — bring in a calibration technician to verify both instrument sets before trusting either.

title: Stop and escalate to a licensed design professional, licensed contractor, or your health authority when:
content: As-built drawings are unavailable and the vessel has complex geometry (multiple hoppers, vanishing edge, tiered levels, integrated spa spillover) that you cannot segment with confidence. Your measured volume differs from the design or permitted volume by more than about 10% and you cannot account for the difference. A metered-fill cross-check will not reconcile, and a leak is suspected — call a leak detection specialist and a licensed contractor. Do not simply add makeup water and keep dosing. The turnover calculation using your measured volume shows the system cannot meet the code-required turnover. This is a design or equipment matter for an engineer and the health authority — not something to resolve by adjusting the volume figure. You are asked to certify or file a volume figure for a permit, plan review, or variance. Filed figures should rest on stamped drawings. Vessel geometry has been altered (resurfacing that changed depths, bench added, ledge installed) — the volume must be recomputed and the recirculation design reviewed. Depth markings or "no diving" markings do not match your measured depths. This is a life-safety discrepancy. Report it immediately and restrict use of the affected area pending review. [S5, S6]

title: Stop and escalate to a licensed contractor, professional engineer, or the health authority when:
content: Measured flow is below the code-required flow and §8.15 troubleshooting does not restore it. Do not keep the vessel open pending a slow diagnosis. Computed pipe velocity substantially exceeds typical guidance, or you observe cavitation, hammer, or persistent air entrainment you cannot trace. Piping modification is an engineer's decision. The required flow meter is missing, unreadable, out of calibration with no service record, or installed in violation of its straight-run requirement. Replacement and correct installation should be done by a qualified contractor. A pump, motor, or VFD requires internal service, rewiring, or setpoint reprogramming beyond your authorization. Electrical work is licensed work.

hierarchy_path: Ch7/Liquid chlorine is labeled by trade percent — available chlorine per unit volume — so it is dosed by volume, not weight. Derive the relationship:
title: Liquid chlorine is labeled by trade percent — available chlorine per unit volume — so it is dosed by volume, not weight. Derive the relationship:
content: Trade percent T means T grams available chlorine per 100 mL = T x 10 grams per liter 1 gallon = 3.785 L Grams per gallon    = T x 10 x 3.785 = T x 37.85 Pounds per gallon   = T x 37.85 / 453.6 = T x 0.08345 lb Now compare that to the Volume Factor for 10,000 gallons (0.0834 lb per ppm). The two constants are numerically the same, which produces a genuinely useful identity: 1 GALLON of sodium hypochlorite at trade percent T, added to 10,000 GALLONS of water, raises free chlorine by approximately T ppm. So one gallon of 12.5% liquid in 10,000 gallons ≈ 12.5 ppm. One gallon of 10% in 10,000 gallons ≈ 10 ppm. Rearranged into a working formula: GALLONS OF LIQUID = Desired ppm change x (Volume in gallons / 10,000) / Trade percent

content: Ultraviolet light in sunlight breaks down free chlorine — a photolytic reaction that destroys the residual regardless of bather load, water balance, or anything else the operator controls. In an unstabilized outdoor vessel under strong sun, a substantial portion of the residual can be lost within hours. On a clear summer day this can be the single largest component of chlorine demand, exceeding bather load and organic oxidation combined. [S17, S18] Chlorinated isocyanurates are markedly more resistant to this photolysis. Chlorine held in the cyanurate reservoir survives sunlight that would have destroyed it in the unbound state, and is released as needed.

title: 17.5.4 Response — physical removal, then oxidation, then filtration
content: STEP 1  PHYSICAL REMOVAL FIRST - this is the effective step - Skim the surface thoroughly - Clean the waterline and tile band per the surface manufacturer's guidance and the product label - Use label-directed absorbent products where appropriate - Empty skimmer and pump baskets STEP 2  OXIDIZE - Verify FC is adequate; correct pH first - Superchlorinate per label and code where the organic load warrants it (Ch 12 sec 12.6, sec 12.7 - superchlorination, NOT hyperchlorination) - A label-directed enzyme product may be used as an adjunct for organic load; follow the label, and note it does not replace oxidation STEP 3  FILTER - Confirm filter condition and clean as needed (17.2.3) - Expect loading from removed organics STEP 4  CORRECT CONTRIBUTING CHEMISTRY - Raise calcium hardness if low (Ch 9 sec 9.14, Ch 11 sec 11.10.4) STEP 5  DILUTE - Where organic and dissolved load is chronic (Ch 9 sec 9.17) STEP 6  SOURCE CONTROL - the actual fix - Enforce pre-swim showering - Ensure deck and equipment cleaning products cannot enter the water - Advise rinsing of laundered swimwear - In spas, avoid quaternary ammonium algaecides

title: 17B.3.5 Water treatment after an animal incident — IF/THEN branches
content: IF  incidental contact only - animal was in the water briefly, NO visible feces, water not fouled, animal appeared healthy THEN 1. Physical cleanup complete (17B.3.4 or live-exit) 2. Brush affected surfaces 3. Test FC, CC, pH; correct pH into band 4. RESTORE the operational residual; if the residual dropped or CC rose, perform an OPERATIONAL SHOCK (17B.2.4) 5. Run circulation and filtration continuously; clean filter as needed 6. Retest full panel; verify clarity 7. Reopen on verified tests per code IF  VISIBLE FECES present, OR the water is heavily fouled, OR the animal was a bird whose droppings are in the water THEN 1. Treat as a FECAL CONTAMINATION EVENT 2. Physically remove ALL visible material by net - never through the filter 3. Apply the FORMED-STOOL-style protocol as a minimum (17B.2.5) 4. Escalate to the DIARRHEAL path if the feces were loose, if the animal appeared ill, if the extent is significant, or if you are in ANY doubt 5. Consult the local health department on which path applies

title: Follow your kit's instruction sheet for sample volume, reagent identities and quantities, drop factors, and the calculation convention. [S11]
content: STEP 1  SAMPLE - Collect per section 18.1: elbow depth, away from returns, immediately - Rinse the titration vessel with the sample water - Measure the sample volume EXACTLY to the mark the kit specifies (the volume determines the factor - see 18.4.4) STEP 2  DEVELOP THE FREE CHLORINE COLOUR - Add the DPD powder/indicator and buffer reagent(s) as the kit directs - Swirl until dissolved. Undissolved powder will end the titration early - A pink colour develops, proportional to free chlorine STEP 3  TITRATE TO A COLOURLESS ENDPOINT - COUNT THE DROPS - Hold the titrant dropper VERTICALLY for consistent drop size - Add ONE drop, swirl, observe. Repeat - SLOW DOWN as the colour fades - the last few drops matter - The endpoint is the FIRST drop at which the pink is COMPLETELY GONE - Record the DROP COUNT FREE CHLORINE = drops x the kit's factor STEP 4  RELEASE THE COMBINED CHLORINE - Add the total-chlorine reagent (iodide-containing) as the kit directs - Swirl and wait the specified time - Pink returns, corresponding to the combined chlorine STEP 5  TITRATE AGAIN - COUNT THESE DROPS SEPARATELY - Continue titrating to a colourless endpoint using the same technique - Record this SECOND drop count separately from the first CALCULATE per your kit's convention: - Many kits: the SECOND drop count x factor = COMBINED CHLORINE, and TOTAL = FREE + COMBINED - Other kits: the second titration yields TOTAL, from which you subtract FREE to get COMBINED **Kits differ. Use YOUR kit's stated calculation. Do not assume.** STEP 6  RECORD - Both drop counts, the sample volume, the factor applied, and the three computed values (FC, CC, TC)

title: Do work these questions in order. The first "yes" is your first action.
content: 1. Is CIRCULATION running and is CLARITY adequate to operate? -> If no: fix that first. Nothing else is meaningful. 2. Is the DISINFECTANT RESIDUAL outside the permitted range? -> If yes: CLOSURE decision, then correct. This is the health barrier. 3. Is pH outside the permitted range? -> If yes: correct. It governs the effectiveness of Step 2. 4. Is ALKALINITY out of range - or is pH failing to hold? -> If yes: alkalinity is the controlling parameter. Fix it. 5. Is COMBINED CHLORINE at or above the action level? -> If yes: verify the reading, correct pH, then oxidize. 6. Is CYANURIC ACID above the code cap? -> If yes: this is a code issue. Plan dilution. It may also be suppressing your active chlorine at an acceptable FC reading. 7. Is CALCIUM HARDNESS out of range, or is the SATURATION INDEX outside band? -> If yes: correct - usually via pH and alkalinity first (Ch 16 sec 16.9). 8. Everything in range? -> Log it anyway. The trend is the diagnostic.

title: Relieve pressure. Open the air relief valve on the filter. Confirm pressure gauges read zero before removing any lid.
content: Remove the strainer pot lid. If it resists, do not pry with a screwdriver against the housing — use the manufacturer's wrench or lid tool. Lift out the basket. Empty debris into the trash, not the floor drain. Inspect the basket for cracks or a broken rim. A cracked basket lets debris pass to the impeller. Replace it; do not run without a basket. Rinse the basket and the pot. Inspect the lid O-ring. Clean it. Lubricate with a manufacturer-approved lubricant only. Replace if flattened, cracked, brittle, or stretched. Reseat the basket squarely. A misseated basket can be crushed by the lid. Refit the lid. Hand-tighten unless the manufacturer specifies otherwise. Over-tightening deforms O-rings and cracks lids. Reopen valves. Prime per 23.4. Restore power, restart, and confirm normal pressure and flow.

content: Bonding ties metallic components in and around the pool to a common electrical potential so that no dangerous voltage difference exists between them. Grounding provides a path to earth. They are different things and both are required by code.

hierarchy_path: Ch23/23.8.5 Wet conditions in the equipment room
title: 23.8.5 Wet conditions in the equipment room
content: Never stand in standing water while operating electrical switches or the panel. Address leaks promptly; a wet equipment room floor is both a slip hazard and an electrical hazard. Keep the panel area clear per code — a clear working space in front of electrical panels is required, not optional storage space. Ensure equipment room lighting works. Diagnosing a pump in the dark with a phone flashlight leads to mistakes.

title: 23.8.6 Lockout / tagout
content: Before opening any pump, strainer pot, or filter: Identify all energy sources — electrical, and stored energy in pressurized water. Shut down the pump at the designated disconnect. Apply lock and tag per your facility's written energy control program. Defeat automation: verify the timer, controller, or building management system cannot restart the pump. Verify de-energization. Relieve pressure via the filter air relief and confirm gauges read zero.

title: 23.9.2 Stop after brief assessment
content: Cavitation noise that does not clear after checking water level and baskets. Flow below code minimum that you cannot restore. Repeated GFCI or overload trips. Persistent air in the strainer pot after O-ring service. Any leak that is worsening.

title: Key operator points:
content: Suction outlet covers must be present, unbroken, properly secured, and not expired per their marked service life. A missing or broken suction outlet cover is an immediate closure condition. Do not operate the pump. Do not modify, remove, or defeat a safety vacuum release system (SVRS), automatic pump shut-off, or vent system. Know the location of the emergency pump shut-off and confirm it is labeled, unobstructed, and functional. Test per your code and record the test. If the emergency shut-off is not labeled or not obviously accessible from the deck, that is a finding to correct today.

title: 23.10 Suction entrapment awareness
content: This is covered in depth elsewhere in this manual, but it belongs in any pump chapter because the pump creates the hazard.

title: What changes for the operator:
content: Flow depends on the programmed speed. A speed change is a flow change and therefore a turnover change. Never change a programmed speed without authorization. Verify the resulting gpm against the code minimum with the flow meter and record it. Confirm that any programmed low-speed period still meets code-required flow. Some codes prohibit dropping below the turnover flow at any time when the facility is open. Confirm that chemical feed and automatic controllers remain within their operating flow window at the lower speed. Erosion feeders and flow switches often have minimum flow requirements. A drive fault code is diagnostic information. Record the exact code text before clearing it; the technician will need it.

title: Record pressure and flow together every round. Interpret them as a pair using the table in 23.7.2.
content: Establish and date a clean filter baseline pressure after every cleaning or media change. Keep the strainer basket clean, intact, and installed. Always. Never throttle the suction side. Never start a pump against a closed discharge. Prime before starting any above-grade pump; stop after one failed prime attempt and diagnose. title: Checklist:
content: [ ] Visually inspect the filter tank exterior for cracks, corrosion, or loose connections. [ ] Check all hose connections (inlet, outlet, backwash/waste lines) for tightness and leaks. [ ] Verify the pressure gauge reads zero or near zero when the pump is off. [ ] Test the pump startup; listen for unusual noise. [ ] Open any isolation or gate valves that may have been closed during the off-season. [ ] Run the pump and monitor for 5–10 minutes; check that water flow is normal. [ ] Verify the backwash/waste line is clear and drains properly (dump bucket test: open waste valve briefly to confirm flow). [ ] Inspect visible media (sand surface, DE powder stored, or cartridge) for degradation or contamination. [ ] Record baseline pressure reading after 10 minutes of circulation.

title: Action:
content: Stop the pump. Open the air bleed valve (if equipped) on the filter tank and let air escape for 30–60 seconds (listen for a hiss). Close the bleed valve. Check the pump strainer basket (the small tank on top of or beside the pump); it should be filled with water, not air. If the strainer is dry, fill it manually or check the pool water level (may be too low to supply water to the pump intake). Restart the pump slowly and observe for 2–3 minutes until pressure stabilizes.

title: Verify pool and spa water temperature with an independent, calibrated thermometer — not only the heater's own display or the controller reading. A heater display reads the water inside the heater, not the water swimmers are in.
content: Confirm the temperature at the pool matches the posted temperature and the facility target. Confirm combustion air openings and louvers are unobstructed. Confirm nothing is stored against, on top of, or in front of the heater. Combustible storage near a gas appliance is a fire hazard and a code violation. Confirm the area around a heat pump's air intake and discharge is clear. Visually check the vent connector where visible: no disconnection, no sag, no visible corrosion holes, no rust streaking at joints. Confirm gas shutoff valve location is known and accessible.

title: 25.2.3 Weekly
content: Verify the flow switch's function is being respected: with the pump off, the heater must not fire. Observe only — do not manipulate the switch. Inspect for scale or corrosion evidence at accessible connections. Confirm heater bonding conductor is intact and connected (visual only). Verify the temperature log has no unexplained gaps. Electrical connection and element inspection.

title: 25.4.3 Spa hyperthermia awareness
content: Operators and lifeguards should recognize that elevated water temperature affects users beyond simple discomfort. Populations at elevated risk from hot water immersion include people who are pregnant, young children, older adults, people with cardiovascular conditions, people with impaired temperature sensation, and people who have consumed alcohol or drugs — including some medications.

hierarchy_path: Ch25/Stop: If a patron or staff member complains about "too much chlorine smell," do not reduce the chlorine feed. That response makes the underlying problem worse. Test, identify combined chlorine and the bather-waste loading, and address the actual cause.
title: Stop: If a patron or staff member complains about "too much chlorine smell," do not reduce the chlorine feed. That response makes the underlying problem worse. Test, identify combined chlorine and the bather-waste loading, and address the actual cause.
content: Exposure to elevated airborne DBPs at indoor pools is associated with: Eye irritation, redness, and burning. Nose and throat irritation. Coughing, wheezing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath. Worsening of asthma symptoms. Headache. Staff who work poolside for full shifts — lifeguards, instructors, coaches, operators — have far greater cumulative exposure than patrons and are the population most likely to show symptoms. NIOSH health hazard evaluations at indoor aquatic facilities have documented respiratory symptom clusters among aquatic staff.

title: Stop — do not:
content: Block, close, cover, or redirect supply diffusers or exhaust grilles, even to stop a draft complaint. Store equipment in front of return or exhaust openings. Prop open doors between the pool space and adjacent occupied areas. Turn off or set back the ventilation system at night or during low occupancy without explicit engineering authorization. Contaminant and moisture generation continue when the pool is unoccupied, and setback has caused documented building damage and air quality failures. Adjust dampers, fan speeds, or HVAC controls.

hierarchy_path: Ch25/Escalate to management and facilities immediately when:
title: Escalate to management and facilities immediately when:
content: Combined chlorine remains above the code maximum across multiple consecutive tests despite chemistry corrections. Two or more staff or patrons report respiratory or eye irritation within a short period. Persistent strong odor in the pool space. Relative humidity persistently outside the target band. Air temperature below water temperature. Visible condensation on building surfaces, or new corrosion or staining on structural metal. Air visibly or perceptibly moving from the pool space into the lobby or locker rooms. Any HVAC alarm, fault, or unit shutdown. A supply diffuser delivering no air.

title: 25.6.7 Carbon monoxide
content: Where fuel-fired equipment serves an indoor facility, carbon monoxide is a distinct and lethal hazard separate from DBPs. Sources include blocked or disconnected flues, cracked heat exchangers, inadequate combustion air, and negative pressure in the equipment room pulling combustion products back into the space.

title: 25.7.2 Setback discipline
content: Water temperature setback overnight saves energy but must be authorized and documented, and recovery time must be planned so the water is at target before the first program. Repeated large swings accelerate scale formation and stress the heater.

hierarchy_path: Ch25/Log free chlorine, total chlorine, and calculated combined chlorine every test — not free chlorine alone.
title: Log free chlorine, total chlorine, and calculated combined chlorine every test — not free chlorine alone.
content: Remember that strong "chlorine smell" means DBPs, not excess chlorine. Never respond by reducing chlorine. Log air temperature, relative humidity, and water temperature on the same time base so the relationship is visible. Confirm air is above water temperature, humidity is in the target band, and diffusers and grilles are clear and unobstructed. Never block a diffuser, prop a pool-space door, or set back ventilation. Test CO alarms monthly and record. On alarm, evacuate first. Treat clustered staff respiratory complaints as an air quality signal requiring documented investigation.

title: Chapter 26 — Routine Maintenance Schedules
content: Chapter 26 — Routine Maintenance Schedules

title: 26.1.2 Setting frequencies
content: Start from the code-required minimum frequency. That is your floor, never your target. Increase frequency for: high bather load, outdoor pools, spas and hot tubs, splash pads and interactive water features, therapy pools, and any feature with aerosol generation. Increase frequency for any item that has failed, drifted, or been cited in the last 12 months. Review the whole schedule annually and after any incident, renovation, or equipment change.

title: 26.1.4 Record retention
content: Keep daily logs on site and immediately available for inspection.

title: 26.2.3 Weekly
content: Test total alkalinity, calcium hardness, and cyanuric acid (outdoor / stabilized pools). Test combined chlorine or total chlorine and calculate combined chlorine.

title: Calculate and record water balance index (see Chapter 11).
content: Calculate and record water balance index (see Chapter 11).

title: 0.7 ppm combined chlorine indicates accumulating chloramines. Investigate bather load, fill-water quality, and disinfection capacity, and treat per Chapter 14.
content: 0.7 ppm combined chlorine indicates accumulating chloramines. Investigate bather load, fill-water quality, and disinfection capacity, and treat per Chapter 14.

title: 26.2.4 Monthly
content: Perform total dissolved solids test and record; compare to the value recorded at the last fill. Test fill/source water for hardness, alkalinity, pH, and (where relevant) iron, copper, and manganese. Replace test kit reagents on the schedule the manufacturer's label specifies, or sooner if results become erratic. Compare a sample against a second, independently sourced test kit or a laboratory result to confirm your kit is reading true. Review the month's logs for trends: creeping pH, rising cyanuric acid, rising combined chlorine, falling flow.

title: 26.2.5 Quarterly and seasonal
content: Send a sample for independent laboratory analysis where your code or risk profile calls for it. Recalculate the required chemical dosages from measured pool volume, not from historical habit.

title: At season open (outdoor) or at each shutdown/restart: drain or partially drain per Chapter 24, clean, refill, rebalance, and record a full startup water panel before opening.
content: At season open (outdoor) or at each shutdown/restart: drain or partially drain per Chapter 24, clean, refill, rebalance, and record a full startup water panel before opening.

title: 26.3.1 Daily
content: Record influent and effluent filter pressure and calculate differential pressure. Record flow rate from the flow meter; compare to the design flow on the permit or nameplate. Empty the pump strainer basket. Look and listen: check for leaks, drips, unusual noise, vibration, hot motor housings, or burning smells. Confirm chemical feed pumps are running, feed lines are intact, and day tanks or drums have adequate volume. Confirm chemical storage separation is intact: no acid and hypochlorite in shared containment, no leaking containers. Verify mechanical room ventilation is operating. Verify eyewash station and emergency shower are unobstructed and flush an eyewash briefly.

title: If the clean-filter differential recorded at startup was 4 psi, this filter has gained 6 psi of resistance. Backwash or clean per Chapter 9 and per the manufacturer's stated differential threshold — commonly 8–10 psi above clean, but the manual controls.
content: If the clean-filter differential recorded at startup was 4 psi, this filter has gained 6 psi of resistance. Backwash or clean per Chapter 9 and per the manufacturer's stated differential threshold — commonly 8–10 psi above clean, but the manual controls.

title: 26.3.2 Weekly
content: Backwash or clean filters when the differential threshold is reached — by pressure, not by calendar. Inspect and clean chemical feeder injection points and check valves. Calibrate or verify the ORP and pH probes on the automated controller against manual test results; clean probes per manufacturer instruction. Inspect the chemical containment areas, secondary containment, and spill kit contents. Inspect the UV or ozone secondary disinfection system indicators and lamp-hour counters, where installed. Check pump seals for weeping. Verify all valves are in their correct normal operating positions and that valve tags are legible.

title: 26.3.3 Monthly
content: Inspect and lubricate equipment per the manufacturer's O&M manual — pumps, motors, valve actuators. Inspect strainer baskets and lids for cracks; replace gaskets and O-rings that are hardened or deformed. Inspect the surge tank or balance tank: water level, cleanliness, float and level controls. Verify the flow meter reads plausibly; clean the sight tube or sensor. Test the emergency shutoff switches for pumps and for any water feature. Inspect chemical storage: labels legible, containers dated, oldest stock used first, no incompatible neighbors. Review and update the mechanical room piping and equipment diagram if anything changed.

title: 26.3.4 Quarterly
content: Open and inspect the filter interior — sand bed depth and channeling, cartridge condition, DE grid condition. Verify pump performance against the pump curve: measured flow at measured head. Inspect heater: burner or heat exchanger condition, venting, combustion air supply, and any manufacturer-specified service. Gas-fired and electric heater service is performed by a licensed technician. Inspect and test the automated controller's alarm and lockout functions. Test the mechanical room chemical vapor or gas detection system, where installed. Review SDS binder for completeness and currency for every chemical on site.

title: 26.3.5 Annual and seasonal
content: Full filter media replacement or deep clean per the manufacturer's interval — sand commonly on a multi-year cycle, cartridges and DE grids more often. Professional electrical inspection: bonding, grounding, GFCI devices, disconnects, motor wiring. Test and record GFCI trip function on all required circuits. Many codes require this monthly as well; follow the more frequent requirement. Backflow preventer testing on the fill line by a certified tester. Heater and boiler annual service by a licensed technician. Verify pool volume by measurement, not by memory, and update all dosage worksheets.

title: Winterization or seasonal shutdown per Chapter 24; seasonal startup per Chapter 25.
content: Winterization or seasonal shutdown per Chapter 24; seasonal startup per Chapter 25.

title: 26.4.1 Daily
content: Walk the full deck perimeter. Remove trip hazards, standing water, debris, and glass. Confirm all required signage is present, legible, and correctly positioned: depth markings, "No Diving," capacity, emergency contact, rules, and where applicable "No lifeguard on duty." Confirm deck drains are clear and draining. Confirm handrails, ladders, and grab rails are present and firmly anchored — grip and pull each one.

title: 26.4.2 Weekly
content: Pressure-wash or deep-clean deck surfaces, with attention to slip resistance in high-traffic paths. Inspect and disinfect showers, changing rooms, and any interactive feature spray heads. Inspect deck expansion joints, caulk, and coping for cracks, lifting, or spalling. Inspect furniture: chairs, tables, umbrellas, lifeguard stands — stability and condition. Inspect fencing and barrier line for gaps, climbable features, loose pickets, and ground clearance. Check that no items have been stored against the barrier that would create a climbing aid.

title: 26.4.3 Monthly
content: Inspect the pool shell, tile, grout, plaster, or liner for cracking, delamination, or hollow spots. Inspect and torque the fasteners on all ladders, rails, starting platforms, diving boards, and slides. Follow the manufacturer's torque spec. Inspect underwater lighting lenses and seals for water intrusion. Inspect deck-to-water transitions, steps, and benches for chipping and sharp edges. Inspect the enclosure, roof, and dehumidification system in indoor facilities; look for condensation damage and corrosion. Verify slip resistance in wet-traffic zones and re-treat or re-surface where degraded.

title: 26.4.4 Annual and seasonal
content: Structural and shell inspection, in an emptied pool where feasible. Diving board, slide, and platform inspection to the manufacturer's specification, by a qualified inspector. Repaint or re-mark depth markings, "No Diving" markings, and step edges. Recoat or resurface deck as needed. Verify barrier height, gate hardware height, and opening dimensions against current code — codes change; your fence did not. Indoor facilities: inspect and service the HVAC and dehumidification system; check air-change rate and duct condition.

title: 26.5.1 Daily
content: Inventory and inspect rescue equipment before opening: reaching pole or shepherd's crook, ring buoy with line, rescue tube, backboard with head immobilizer and straps. Confirm equipment is mounted in its designated position, unobstructed, and immediately reachable. Confirm the first aid kit is stocked to your posted list and nothing is expired. Confirm the AED is present, the status indicator shows ready, and pads are unexpired and sealed. Confirm the emergency telephone or communication device is present and functional — place a test call or verify dial tone. Confirm the emergency action plan is posted and legible. Confirm bloodborne pathogen and body-fluid cleanup supplies are stocked. Confirm lifeguard coverage matches the posted staffing plan, or that "No Lifeguard on Duty" signage is correctly posted.

title: 26.5.3 Monthly
content: Test the AED per the manufacturer's schedule; record the self-test result and battery status. Replace expired first aid and PPE stock. Run a documented emergency drill: distressed swimmer, submerged victim, spinal injury, chemical release, or severe weather. Rotate scenarios. Verify all staff certifications remain current; flag anything expiring within 90 days. Test the emergency lighting and any emergency power system. Review the incident log for the month; identify patterns and corrective actions.

title: 26.5.4 Quarterly and annual
content: Full documented emergency action plan review with all staff. In-service training on rescue skills, CPR/AED, oxygen administration, and chemical handling. Replace rescue equipment showing any UV damage, deformation, or wear — replace, do not repair. Annual review of the emergency action plan against current code and current facility layout. Annual confirmation that local emergency services have current facility access information and chemical inventory where required.

title: 26.7 Log design requirements
content: Every log form must contain: Facility name and pool/feature identifier. Date and time of each entry. The measured value or the completion checkbox — not "OK" alone for anything measurable. Units for every number. Initials of the person performing the task. A corrective action field adjacent to every measurable field. A supervisor review signature line with a defined review frequency. Do not use a log that only records passing results. A log with no out-of-range entries over a full season is evidence of poor recording, not perfect operation.

title: Key checks
content: Disinfectant residual, pH, clarity, and flow verified before every opening and at code frequency during operation. Filter cleaned on differential pressure, not on the calendar. Every drain and suction outlet cover present, intact, and secured — checked daily. Every barrier gate self-closes and self-latches — checked daily. Rescue equipment, AED, first aid, and emergency communication verified daily. Controller readings verified against a manual test kit daily. Every task has an owner, a frequency, a recorded result, and a corrective-action path.

title: Common mistakes
content: Treating code minimum frequencies as targets rather than floors. Trusting an automated controller without daily manual verification. Backwashing on a fixed weekly schedule regardless of differential pressure — wasting water and media life, or running a blinded filter for days. Recording "OK" instead of a number, which destroys the ability to see trends. Back-filling logs at the end of the shift or week from memory. Adding a full calculated chemical dose at once instead of staging and retesting. Storing supplies or furniture against a barrier, creating a climbing aid. Letting a task list live in one person's head; when they leave, the program leaves. Keeping a log with no out-of-range entries and believing it. Deferring a barrier, drain cover, or rescue equipment repair as "non-urgent."

title: When to call a professional
content: Call a licensed or certified specialist — do not perform in-house — for: Any electrical work, bonding, grounding, or GFCI device replacement. Gas-fired heater, boiler, or combustion venting service. Backflow preventer testing and certification. Structural repair of the shell, deck, or coping. Diving board, slide, or platform inspection and repair to manufacturer specification. Suction outlet cover replacement or any change to the suction system, including VGB compliance work. HVAC and dehumidification system service in indoor facilities. Chemical release or spill exceeding your spill kit capacity and staff training. Any repair the equipment manufacturer's manual reserves to authorized service. Any condition where you are uncertain whether the facility is safe to open. When uncertain, stay closed.

content: INHALATION   — Move to fresh air immediately. Do not send anyone unprotected back in. Keep the person calm and at rest. Call 911 for any shortness of breath, coughing, chest tightness, or hoarseness. Delayed pulmonary effects are possible; EMS evaluation even if the person "feels fine." SKIN         — Remove contaminated clothing (cut it off rather than pulling it over the head/face). Flush with copious tepid water at the safety shower for the duration the SDS states, typical educational target minimum 15 minutes. Do not apply neutralizers or creams. EYE          — Eyewash immediately. Hold eyelids open. Flush minimum 15 minutes, or per SDS. Remove contact lenses if easily removable. Do not delay flushing to find the SDS — start water, then read. INGESTION    — Do NOT induce vomiting. Rinse mouth. Call 911 and Poison Control. Bring the container/label or SDS to EMS. ALL CASES    — Give EMS the product name and the SDS. Document exposure time, duration, flush time, and symptoms. File the injury/illness record required by your occupational safety rules.

hierarchy_path: Ch29/30.7.5 EAP — chemical overfeed or off-gassing at the pool
title: 30.7.5 EAP — chemical overfeed or off-gassing at the pool
content: 1. Clear the water immediately and clear the deck to fresh air. 2. Shut off the chemical feeder(s). Shut off the circulation pump if the plan directs it, or if feeding continues. 3. Do not enter the equipment room if there is a chlorine odor or haze. 4. Ventilate the pool enclosure — open doors, run exhaust — from outside. 5. Call 911 if anyone is symptomatic or the odor is strong. 6. Test water only when it is safe to approach; expect extreme pH or disinfectant readings. 7. Notify the health authority. Closure is required until chemistry is verified in range and the cause is corrected. 8. Document: feeder settings, tank levels, timer/controller log, ORP/pH trend, who was in the water, symptoms reported. Indoor facilities: a chlorine odor in the natatorium is not "the smell of a clean pool." It is a signal — chloramines, a feed fault, or a ventilation failure. Investigate it every time.

title: Two or more patrons report rash, ear, respiratory, or gastrointestinal illness within a short window — notify the health authority immediately, do not investigate alone.
content: Any suspected Legionella case is associated with your facility. This is a public health investigation, not a maintenance task. You cannot hold minimum residual at design bather load even with the feeder at maximum — this indicates undersized feed equipment, inadequate turnover, or plumbing biofilm requiring assessment. Measured turnover cannot meet code after filter service and pump verification — hydraulic or equipment sizing review is needed. A suction outlet cover is missing, damaged, expired, or of unknown specification — a certified installer must address entrapment protection. The heater, thermostat, or high-limit device fails or behaves erratically — licensed gas/electrical service only. Persistent scale, staining, or corrosion that survives normal balance correction — water analysis and surface assessment.

title: The critical distinction is formed vs diarrheal, not animal vs human, and not large vs small. [S-CDC-HS] [S-MAHC]
content: 1. Is the contamination DIARRHEAL, dispersed, or of UNKNOWN type? YES -> HIGH-RISK RESPONSE. Close the venue. Assume chlorine-tolerant protozoa may be present. Follow your code's elevated disinfection procedure (commonly hyperchlorination held for a specified CT). Notify the AHJ. Go to §34.6.5. NO  -> continue 2. Is it a CARCASS? YES -> Go to §34.7 (removal, then assess as contamination based on condition and species). NO  -> continue 3. Is the animal a species your AHJ or state advisory flags as elevated risk in recreational water (varies by jurisdiction and region)? YES -> Follow the AHJ / advisory response, which may require the elevated procedure. When in doubt, ask before deciding. NO  -> continue 4. It is FORMED animal droppings. -> STANDARD RESPONSE. Remove intact, disinfect the removal tool, raise free chlorine and hold at correct pH for the contact time your code specifies, filter, verify, then reopen. Go to §34.6.4. content: This is the most important idea in the chapter. A shortcut gets taken once because of time pressure. Nothing bad happens. It gets taken again. Nothing happens. Within months it is simply how the venue operates, and nobody remembers it was ever a deviation. The absence of consequences is read as evidence of safety, when it was only ever evidence of luck. It sounds like: "We've always run it that way." "The controller's close enough." "We test twice a day, that's been fine." "That gate sticks, everyone knows to pull it." "We don't have time for the full contact time, and nobody's ever gotten sick." "The inspector never looks at that."

title: Countermeasures:
content: Self-inspect against the AHJ's own criteria, on a schedule, honestly. Treat a procedure you have drifted from as a finding, not a preference. A navigational bridge between this manual's topics and the corresponding themes in the CDC Model Aquatic Health Code (MAHC), so an operator studying a topic here can find the related material there. This map is not a legal substitute. The MAHC is a model code. It is guidance developed by CDC with stakeholder input; it is not federal law and has no legal force on its own. It becomes enforceable only where a state, county, or municipality adopts it — in whole, in part, or with modifications. Many jurisdictions have not adopted it at all and operate under their own code. Your enforceable requirements come from your local health code and your AHJ. Neither this manual nor the MAHC overrides them. Use this map to find related concepts and build understanding — never to determine compliance. On section numbers. This map deliberately references themes and module-level areas rather than specific section numbers. MAHC numbering has changed across editions, and a citation to a stale section number is worse than no citation — it looks authoritative and sends the reader to the wrong place. Verify against the current edition at the CDC MAHC page before relying on any locator. How to use this map. Find your topic in the left column. The right column tells you which area of the MAHC to search and what concepts to look for. Then read the MAHC's Annex for that area — the Annex carries the technical rationale, and it is generally more useful to an operator trying to understand why than the code language itself.
